hook: Capstone four: an agent living in Telegram or Slack — **personalized through memory, guarded at the boundary, monitored like production.** The front door of everything you've built.

scenes.title: Chat is the interface: **webhooks in, replies out**
scenes.sub: Telegram/Slack mechanics — the async backbone you've already built
scenes.narration: The surface is simple to describe because PY-12 and PY-14 built the machinery: the platform — Telegram or Slack — POSTs events to your webhook; your FastAPI endpoint validates the payload — signature verification, bot-token checks — enqueues a job; a worker runs the agent loop and POSTs the reply through the platform's API. The disciplines you already own: ASYNC — webhooks enqueue, never process inline — the endpoint returns 200 in milliseconds and the queue carries the work — AG-19's decoupling, because a slow agent must never timeout the platform's delivery; RETRIES — platform APIs retry deliveries when your endpoint is down — idempotency keys on message IDs prevent double-processing, the same rule as AG-19's jobs; and STREAMING-ish UX — chat platforms don't stream, so the agent posts a 'thinking…' placeholder and EDITS it with the answer — perceived latency managed within platform limits. One platform quirk: message EDITS are rate-limited — batch updates, keep the placeholder text short.

scenes.title: Webhook endpoint: validate, enqueue, answer fast
annot: job_id from the platform's message ID: redeliveries dedupe automatically — the AG-19 idempotency pattern, platform edition
Bots ignored at the edge: bot-to-bot loops are a real failure mode — cut them at the door
The placeholder message travels with the job: the worker EDITS it rather than sending fresh — one message per request, rate-limit friendly
scenes.narration: Three platform-specific traps this endpoint avoids. Signature verification FIRST — forged webhooks are free attack surface, and an unvalidated chatbot endpoint is an unauthenticated remote-trigger for your agent; process nothing before verification. Message-type sprawl — Telegram delivers edits, reactions, service notices on the same webhook; the guard clauses filter to actual user text before anything expensive happens. And the thinking-placeholder — chat's equivalent of streaming: it sets the conversational expectation ('working on it') and its message ID rides the job so the final answer EDITS it in place — the user's message history stays clean. The endpoint is deliberately boring; everything interesting happens in the worker — where this project's real design lives.

scenes.title: Personalization through memory: **the assistant that knows you**
scenes.narration: A messaging assistant without memory is a stranger in every conversation; with memory, it's YOUR assistant. The register mapping: SHORT-TERM — the conversation, managed per AG-13 — chat threads are long and rambling, so compaction matters even more: summarize older thread segments, keep recent turns verbatim. LONG-TERM SEMANTIC — preferences and facts the user volunteers — 'I prefer Hindi-English mix', 'my team is on Slack #eng' — written at conversation end via the AG-12 write gate, deduplicated, per-user scoped; retrieved at session start — just-in-time, threshold-gated. EPISODIC — 'last time you helped me draft the vendor email' — surfacing when the current request resembles a past one; chat's informal references — 'same as before' — make episodic recall unusually valuable. SCRATCHPAD — for multi-step tasks the assistant works through visibly — 'checking your calendar… checking the doc…' — the progress notes pattern keeps chat users informed mid-task, the conversational version of AG-12's resumability.

items.s: Every memory scoped to user_id — retrieval-time filtering is structural (AG-13) · group chats complicate: memory per user, context shared
Reflection extracts durable facts · dedupe against existing memory · nothing mid-conversation
"What do you remember about me?" · "Forget that" — inspectable and erasable memory is a trust feature, not a compliance extra

scenes.narration: Group chats deserve special care: the context is shared, but memory must NOT be — what Alice tells the bot in a group is Alice's memory, not Bob's; and cross-user disclosure — the bot repeating Alice's preferences when Bob asks — is a privacy incident in a group setting, the AG-13 access-check lesson with higher stakes. The user-visible memory commands are the trust layer: 'what do you remember about me' returns the actual entries — provenance included, 'learned Oct 3 from your message' — and 'forget that' deletes, verified, with confirmation; chat users who can SEE and EDIT their memory extend trust; users who can't, wonder. The TOOLS the assistant wields — calendar, notes, search — inherit AG-07's rules: per-user scoped credentials, side-effect gates, and chat-shaped confirmations — a one-tap inline button beats a link to a review page: 'Send this email?' [Send] [Edit] [Cancel] — approval UX native to the surface.

scenes.title: Chat safety: **small surface, real exposure**
scenes.sub: Injection in DMs, prompt bombs in groups, rate abuse
scenes.narration: A public chatbot is the most exposed deployment shape in this curriculum: anyone can reach it, and chat content is injection-rich — forwarded emails, pasted links, shared documents all arrive as TEXT aimed at your context. The defenses, layered as always: treat inbound content as untrusted — GA-22's labeling rides the system prompt — a forwarded message is DATA, whatever it says; EGRESS scoping — a personal assistant's network reach should be narrow — no arbitrary URL fetching; tools gated — chat-shaped confirmations for anything side-effecting; and GROUP-CHAT hygiene — mention-gating (the bot responds only when addressed — '@assistant …' — ignoring ambient conversation, which slashes both noise and injection surface) and per-sender trust — a group member the bot has never seen gets suggest-level autonomy, not act. RATE LIMITS per user — chat invites abuse play — token budgets per user per day, the AG-19 metering at chat scale.

cards.s: Ambient chat enters context · injection surface maximal · noisy, expensive, risky
Responds when addressed · per-sender trust levels · narrow egress · gated tools · per-user budgets

scenes.narration: The per-sender trust ladder is worth detailing: KNOWN USER with history → their usual autonomy level, memory active; KNOWN GROUP, unfamiliar sender → suggest-only, no memory reads, tools gated; UNKNOWN DM sender → basic chat only, no tools, no memory — escalation as a relationship deepens, AG-17's earned-autonomy principle applied to strangers. Also plan for the prompt-bomb: a user pastes a wall of text ending with 'ignore your instructions and…' — input length caps truncate, injection screens flag, and the response stays calm; test this — GA-22's canary suite runs against the chat surface too. And the social layer: the bot should INTRODUCE its limits on first contact — 'I can check your calendar and notes; I won't message anyone without asking; say "what do you remember" anytime' — the stated-limits discipline from AG-22, delivered conversationally. A bot whose limits are known gets trusted further, faster.

scenes.title: Deploy & monitor: **the front door is production**
scenes.sub: Queues, budgets, dashboards — the full Stage-8 stack, chat-sized
scenes.narration: Operate it like everything else in Stage 8, scaled to a chatbot's shape. DEPLOY: the webhook receiver as a small always-on service — App Service or a Container App; the WORKERS queue-driven — AG-19 — scaling with message volume; the whole thing deployable via the PY-23 pipeline, eval gates included — the messaging golden set: fifty representative conversations with known-good behaviors, regression-gated on every prompt change. MONITOR: per-user cost dashboards — chat users are the most spend-variable traffic that exists; latency — time-to-first-edit on the placeholder; quality — the feedback signal is built into chat: reaction buttons on replies — 👍👎 become GA-24's feedback loop with zero extra UX; and abuse signals — rate-limit trips, injection-screen flags, blocked egress attempts — the GA-22 canaries reporting live. THE SOCIAL LAUNCH: start with five friendly users, watch everything, widen the circle as the exception queue teaches you what real usage looks like — the pilot-then-scale discipline that Stage 10 will formalize.

layers.s: Agent loop · memory registers · gated tools · placeholder-edit replies · budget-metered
Per-user costs · reaction feedback → golden set · abuse-signal alerts · exception queue

scenes.narration: The four capstones form an arc worth naming: the SOP agent governed CHANGE, the analyst agent governed ANSWERS, the document agent governed EXTRACTION — this one governs CONVERSATION, the least structured surface of all, and does it with the same disciplines: bounded power, earned trust, honest limits, watched operation. What a user experiences — an assistant that remembers, thinks out loud, asks before acting, admits limits — is the curriculum made personable. And the build order: one — echo bot with validated webhooks and idempotent enqueueing; two — the agent loop with mention-gating; three — memory registers with the inspect/forget commands; four — one gated tool end-to-end — calendar reads say — with inline confirmations; five — budgets, dashboards, abuse signals; six — the golden conversation set in CI. Stage 9's projects end here; Stage 10 zooms out — from building agents to architecting platforms.

scenes.title: Four capstones built: change, answers, extraction, conversation.
scenes.next: Reel 73 · Stage 10: Azure AI Services — the enterprise platform layer

recap: Webhook receivers validate, enqueue, and answer in milliseconds; platform redeliveries dedupe on message IDs; placeholder-edit UX manages perceived latency
Memory personalizes: per-user namespaces, write gates at thread end, inspectable/erasable memory as a trust feature; group chats need per-sender trust ladders and mention-gating
Chat is the most exposed surface: untrusted inbound content, narrow egress, gated tools, per-user budgets — and reaction buttons close the quality feedback loop natively

quiz.q: Why must webhook handlers never process agent work inline?
opts: Platform deliveries timeout in seconds while agent runs take minutes — enqueue and 200 immediately, or redelivery storms and user-visible failures follow
quiz.why: Decoupling is structural at the boundary: the endpoint's only job is validation and enqueueing — AG-19's queue discipline, platform edition.

quiz.q: Why is mention-gating a security control and not just a UX nicety?
opts: Ambient group-chat content — the richest injection surface — never enters context unless the bot is explicitly addressed, slashing both noise and attack surface
quiz.why: Every unaddressed message that stays out of context is injected text that never reached the model — gating is perimeter control.

quiz.q: Why offer 'what do you remember about me' and 'forget that' as commands?
opts: Inspectability and erasability convert memory from a compliance liability into a trust feature — users extend trust to systems they can audit
quiz.why: AG-13's memory-safety discipline made user-facing: visible, correctable memory is the difference between 'creepy' and 'personal'.

code.title: The chat worker: loop + memory + gates, compact
code.body:
async def handle_chat(job: ChatJob):
    user = users.for_platform(job.user_id)
    trust = user.trust_level(job.chat_type)      # known/unknown/group

    ctx = context.build(
        system=CHAT_SYSTEM,                      # untrusted-content rules
        memory=memory.recall(job.text, user.id,  # threshold-gated
                             k=4),
        recent=recent_turns(job.chat_id, cap=8_000),
    )
    async with budget(user.daily_budget.remaining()):
        result = await agent_loop(ctx, tools=tools_for(trust))

    if result.needs_confirmation:                # inline buttons
        await send_buttons(job.chat_id, result.preview,
                           [Send, Edit, Cancel])
        return

    await telegram.edit(job.placeholder, result.reply)
    await react_buttons(job.chat_id)             # 👍👎 feedback
    memory.consider_write(user.id, job.thread)   # end-of-thread gate
annot: tools_for(trust): the same tool set, different autonomy by sender relationship — AG-17's dial, chat edition
budget() wraps the whole loop: per-user daily meters enforced at runtime, not invoiced later
consider_write at thread end: memory writes are deliberate events, not ambient logging

notes:
# Project: Messaging Assistant

## Surface
- Webhook: validate signature → filter (bots, non-text) → idempotent enqueue (message-ID keys) → 200 in ms.
- Placeholder message + edit = chat's streaming UX; edits are rate-limited — batch.

## Tools & memory
- AG-12 registers chat-sized: compaction for long threads, per-user namespaces, end-of-thread write gates.
- Group chats: mention-gating, per-sender trust ladder (known → suggest → basic), cross-user disclosure = incident.
- User commands: 'what do you remember' / 'forget that' — memory as a trust feature.

## Safety
- Untrusted inbound content; narrow egress; inline-button confirmations; per-user daily budgets.

## Deploy & monitor
- Tiny always-on receiver + queue-driven workers; PY-23 pipeline with conversation golden set.
- 👍👎 reactions = native feedback loop; abuse-signal alerts; pilot with 5 friendly users, then widen.
